summary: Gives guidelines for designers of unicast applications that use UDP, with a main focus on congestion control, since UDP has none of its own. This is a Best Current Practice, and it was replaced by RFC 8085.

eli5.summary: Cars on a road need to slow down when traffic builds up. UDP has no brakes, so this memo tells program makers how to add their own. It was later replaced by RFC 8085.

subtitle: Rules of thumb for programs that use UDP, starting with: bring your own congestion control.

tldr.problem: UDP has no congestion control, so applications that use it can send at the line rate of the link and contribute to congestion collapse or unfairness to other traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The document gives guidelines for unicast UDP applications on congestion control, message size, reliability, checksums, middlebox traversal, sockets programming and ICMP, and recommends an IETF transport such as TCP, SCTP or DCCP where possible.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that has since been obsoleted by RFC 8085, which is the version to follow.

facts.label: Keep-alive minimum interval
facts.value: Not more than once every 15 seconds

today: RFC 5405 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 8085. Read the newer document for current guidance on using UDP.

sections.title: Why UDP Needs Guidelines
sections.content:
UDP is a minimal, unreliable, best-effort message transport with no connection setup or teardown. That makes it efficient, but it also provides no inherent congestion control. On many platforms an application can send UDP datagrams at the line rate of its link, which is often far above the available path capacity.

The RFC cites RFC 2914 for two reasons congestion control matters: preventing congestion collapse (more load, less useful work) and establishing a degree of fairness between flows. Even slow rates matter: five 1500-byte datagrams in one second can already exceed a 56 Kb/s path.

The guidelines cover unicast applications only. Multicast, broadcast and anycast uses need expertise beyond this document. If an application does not follow a guideline, it is RECOMMENDED that the designers document the reason in the application's specification.
sections.eli5: If every car on a road drives as fast as it can, nobody gets anywhere. UDP lets programs do that, so the programs have to be polite on their own.

sections.title: Congestion Control Guidelines
sections.content:
Applications MUST NOT assume anything about path characteristics. The RECOMMENDED alternative to custom UDP mechanisms is an IETF transport such as TCP, SCTP or DCCP. If an application sticks with UDP, it SHOULD control its sending rate across all the UDP traffic to a destination, even if it uses several sockets or processes.

  • Bulk transfer: applications SHOULD implement TFRC (RFC 5348), window-based TCP-like control, or otherwise compete fairly with TCP within an order of magnitude. Unadaptive behavior SHOULD NOT be the default.
  • Low data volume: applications SHOULD send on average no more than one datagram per round-trip time, keep a smoothed RTT estimate following RFC 2988, and back off their retransmission timer exponentially on loss. An initial value of 3 seconds is RECOMMENDED. Without an RTT estimate they MAY use a predetermined interval, and with no return traffic at all they SHOULD NOT send more than one datagram every 3 seconds.
  • Tunnels: a UDP tunnel carrying congestion-controlled IP traffic SHOULD NOT add its own congestion control. One carrying non-IP or uncontrolled traffic SHOULD employ it.

Applications that communicate in both directions SHOULD control congestion in both directions.
sections.eli5: If you are sending lots of mail, watch how fast the post office keeps up and slow down when it gets clogged. If you send only a letter now and then, wait a few seconds between tries.

sections.title: Message Size, Reliability and Checksums
sections.content:
Message size. Fragmentation lowers reliability, since losing one fragment loses the whole packet, and some NATs and firewalls drop fragments. Applications SHOULD NOT send UDP datagrams that make IP packets larger than the path MTU, and SHOULD use path MTU information or do path MTU discovery. Without it they SHOULD stay under the default effective MTU for sending: for IPv4 the smaller of 576 bytes and the first-hop MTU, and for IPv6 1280 bytes. To find the payload size, applications MUST subtract the IP header and the 8-byte UDP header from the PMTU.

Reliability. Applications that need reliable delivery MUST implement it themselves, and those that need ordering MUST restore it. They SHOULD handle duplicate datagrams, and SHOULD be robust to delayed or duplicate packets within a 2-minute Maximum Segment Lifetime, the same value as TCP.

Checksums. The 16-bit one's complement checksum is relatively weak, so applications needing integrity SHOULD add checks such as a CRC. Applications SHOULD enable UDP checksums, and the checksum is REQUIRED over IPv6. UDP-Lite lets applications that tolerate damaged payloads deliver them instead of discarding them, by turning the length field into a checksum coverage length.
sections.eli5: Keep parcels small enough to fit in the mailbox without being cut up. The post office will not tell you if a parcel is lost, copied or late, so keep your own checklist.

sections.title: Middleboxes, Sockets and ICMP
sections.content:
Middleboxes. NATs and firewalls keep per-flow state for UDP and drop it after a quiet period. Applications SHOULD handle such failures gracefully and be able to re-establish sessions. Keep-alive messages are NOT RECOMMENDED for general use, but specialized applications MAY send them, SHOULD NOT send them more often than once every 15 seconds, and are RECOMMENDED to add slight random jitter. NATs require a state timeout of 2 minutes or longer according to the RFC, though many deployed middleboxes use shorter ones.

Programming. A UDP socket can receive from many source addresses, so applications that care MUST check the source themselves. Responses SHOULD use a source address matching the request's destination address. A zero-length payload is a valid datagram. Connecting a UDP socket is only a local operation. UDP has no flow control, and no TIME-WAIT state, so a later program on the same port may receive delayed packets.

ICMP. Applications SHOULD check that an ICMP message matches a datagram they actually sent, and SHOULD NOT abort on transient 'unreachable' messages.
sections.eli5: Doorkeepers along the way forget you if you stay quiet for too long. You can wave occasionally, but not too often, and be ready to introduce yourself again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
UDP provides no communications security. Applications needing protection against eavesdropping, tampering or forgery SHOULD use end-to-end security from other IETF protocols. Applications that answer short requests with large responses are open to amplification attacks and SHOULD authenticate the sender first, because a source IP address can be spoofed.

The options named are IPsec, which can authenticate or encrypt UDP headers and payloads, and Datagram TLS (DTLS), which encrypts payloads but not the UDP headers. It is RECOMMENDED to use well-known standard mechanisms such as DTLS or IPsec instead of inventing new ones. The document says its congestion control guidelines raise no additional security concerns.
sections.eli5: A postcard can be read by anyone and the return address can be faked, so private messages need a sealed envelope that is made by experts.

viz.caption: CONGESTION GUIDANCE BY KIND OF UDP APPLICATION

cells: SHOULD use TFRC or TCP-like control, or compete fairly with TCP within an order of magnitude
SHOULD send at most one datagram per RTT on average, with exponential back-off
MAY use a predetermined interval, exponentially backed off on loss
SHOULD NOT send more than one datagram every 3 seconds
SHOULD NOT add its own congestion control
